artifacts.title: Referral Note from Family Physician
artifacts.author: Dr. S. Nguyen, Family Medicine
artifacts.body: Mr. Moretti is a 62-year-old male referred for evaluation of rising PSA. Two years of PSA tracking show an increase from 3.1 to 6.8 ng/mL, with a repeat value of 6.5 ng/mL six weeks later. Digital rectal exam deferred in office; recommend urology perform DRE as part of workup. No gross hematuria, dysuria, or fever reported. Patient endorses nocturia and weak urinary stream for approximately 18 months. Family history significant for paternal prostate cancer (deceased age 74) and a brother treated for prostate cancer at age 60. Referred to Urology for further workup including consideration of prostate MRI and possible biopsy.

objectives.text: Correctly interpret a rising PSA trend in context of a confounder (recent vigorous cycling) and recommend appropriate repeat testing conditions rather than reacting to a single value.
Elicit and synthesize prostate cancer risk factors (family history in father and brother, DRE findings obtained via urology's own exam) to risk-stratify and justify imaging before biopsy.
Recommend multiparametric prostate MRI prior to biopsy per current guideline-concordant shared decision-making, explaining what MRI adds (PI-RADS risk stratification) before proceeding to biopsy.

Screen for erectile dysfunction using IIEF-5, and through sensitive, rapport-based direct questioning, uncover the patient's hidden fear that treatment will worsen sexual function, incorporating this into counseling and shared decision-making.
Assess lower urinary tract symptoms using a validated tool (IPSS) and distinguish benign prostatic hyperplasia symptoms from cancer risk indicators.
Correct patient misconceptions about PSA (that any elevation equals cancer) using clear, non-technical language appropriate to health literacy.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Rising PSA (3.1→6.8, repeat 6.5 ng/mL) with moderate LUTS (IPSS 18/35) in a 62-year-old man with strong family history of prostate cancer (father, brother) and benign-feeling prostate on DRE — findings warrant risk-stratified workup with prostate MRI before biopsy decision, in the context of coexisting mild-moderate erectile dysfunction that must be addressed in counseling.
differential: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) causing LUTS, independent contributor to or coincidental with PSA elevation
PSA elevation partly confounded by vigorous exercise (stationary cycling) prior to first draw
Prostatitis (less likely given normal UA, no fever/dysuria, non-tender prostate)
Age-related erectile dysfunction, possibly vascular or related to anxiety, independent of prostate pathology
keyFindings: PSA rose from 3.1 to 6.8 ng/mL over 2 years, repeat 6.5 ng/mL confirming elevation after excluding acute exercise effect
DRE (performed by urology): moderately enlarged, smooth prostate, no nodule/asymmetry
Normal urinalysis excluding infection/hematuria as cause
IPSS 18/35 (moderate), dominant symptoms nocturia x3 and weak stream, consistent with BPH component
First-degree family history: father died of prostate cancer age 74, brother treated age 60 — qualifies for higher-risk category justifying earlier/more aggressive workup

IIEF-5 score 15/25: mild-to-moderate erectile dysfunction; patient's underlying fear that procedures will worsen this is uncovered only through direct, sensitive questioning, not the questionnaire itself
No red-flag symptoms: no hematuria, dysuria, fever, bone pain, or weight loss
plan: Explain to patient that PSA is a screening marker, not diagnostic for cancer; elevation can result from BPH, prostate size, age, and transient factors like vigorous exercise, but a persistently elevated repeat value after accounting for exercise still warrants further workup given family history
Perform digital rectal exam as part of urology's own evaluation rather than relying solely on the referring note
Order multiparametric prostate MRI (PI-RADS scoring) prior to any biopsy decision to risk-stratify and guide targeted biopsy if indicated

If MRI shows a suspicious lesion (PI-RADS 3-5) or risk remains elevated by calculator, proceed to MRI-targeted (+/- systematic) prostate biopsy, performed by urology; discuss biopsy risks (bleeding, infection, transient worsening of urinary/erectile symptoms) explicitly

Address LUTS: discuss BPH management options (watchful waiting, alpha-blocker, 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor) separate from cancer workup; advise discontinuing or disclosing saw palmetto use since it is unregulated, has no established effect on PSA, and is not a periprocedural bleeding risk requiring special guidance before MRI or biopsy, but its use should still be documented and discussed as part of a complete medication history

Directly and sensitively ask about erectile function and any fears about how treatment might affect it; validate the patient's fear once uncovered, explain that pre-existing mild-moderate ED exists independent of any procedure, discuss that treatment approaches (active surveillance, surgery, radiation if cancer found) carry different sexual side-effect profiles, and that this will be part of shared decision-making if cancer is diagnosed
Encourage open conversation with spouse about sexual health concerns if patient is comfortable; offer referral to sexual health counseling or further ED workup as appropriate within urology scope
Advise against repeating PSA immediately after vigorous exercise or ejaculation in the future to avoid false elevation on surveillance labs
Set a realistic timeline for MRI scheduling and follow-up discussion of results before the patient's work travel in 6 weeks, with contingency plan if results are not back in time
Document family history clearly as it affects future screening recommendations for other male relatives
redFlags: Any new bone pain, unexplained weight loss, or gross hematuria would warrant urgent re-evaluation for possible locally advanced or metastatic disease
Palpable nodule or asymmetry on DRE (not present here) would increase urgency and likelihood of biopsy regardless of MRI timing
Rapidly rising PSA velocity could suggest aggressive disease and should prompt expedited rather than routine-interval workup
educationPoints: PSA is organ-specific but not cancer-specific; BPH, prostatitis, recent ejaculation, vigorous exercise, and even recent catheterization can transiently or chronically raise PSA
Multiparametric MRI with PI-RADS scoring before biopsy improves detection of clinically significant cancer and can reduce unnecessary biopsies of low-risk disease
First-degree relatives with prostate cancer, especially diagnosed at younger age (brother at 60), meaningfully raise lifetime risk and lower the threshold for earlier, more thorough workup

Shared decision-making requires explicitly asking about sexual function and underlying fears, since a questionnaire alone will not surface emotionally sensitive concerns that many men will not volunteer due to embarrassment or stoicism

All major treatment options for localized prostate cancer (surgery, radiation, active surveillance) carry different but real risks to erectile and urinary function, and this should be discussed before, not after, a biopsy result changes the conversation

mismatches.patientClaim: Frank reports he rides the stationary bike most mornings as a regular habit, and specifically rode vigorously the morning of his first elevated PSA draw (6.8 ng/mL) — a detail he volunteers only when asked directly about exercise around the time of testing.
mismatches.recordEvidence: The PSA trend table (d1/a1) shows only bare values and draw dates: 6.8 ng/mL three months ago and a repeat 6.5 ng/mL six weeks later with no exercise history recorded. The repeat draw, obtained without any noted pre-draw exertion, remained elevated at 6.5, showing that exercise only partially explains the picture and a true PSA elevation persists.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Learners should recognize that while vigorous exercise can transiently elevate PSA, this history must be actively elicited from the patient rather than read off a lab report; a repeat value drawn without that confounder remaining significantly elevated confirms a true abnormality requiring further workup, not dismissal of the result.

mismatches.patientClaim: Frank says he started saw palmetto about 4 months ago, after being told his PSA was high, implying it could not have caused the initial elevation but might be an attempt to self-treat.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Medication list (d5) lists saw palmetto as a current supplement but has no column or entry for when it was started. The PSA trend (d1) shows PSA was already elevated at 4.4 ng/mL one year ago, well before the patient's reported 4-month supplement start, so the trend predates and is independent of the supplement regardless of its exact start date.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Medication lists often capture only current status, not start dates; clarifying the timeline of supplement use relative to lab draws by direct questioning prevents incorrectly attributing or dismissing PSA changes to unregulated OTC products.

profile.title: Rising PSA with strong family history in a 62-year-old man with erectile concerns
profile.summary: A 62-year-old building contractor with PSA rising from 3.1 to 6.8 ng/mL over two years presents for results discussion. He has moderate LUTS, strong family history (father died of prostate cancer at 74, brother treated at 60), and unspoken erectile dysfunction fears. The case teaches risk-stratified workup with MRI before biopsy, interpreting PSA trends with confounders (cycling), distinguishing BPH symptoms from cancer risk, and sensitively eliciting hidden concerns about sexual function in shared decision-making.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit; patient's home office in Philadelphia
